# Preliminary Report.

Simon the Magician founded a heresy, assisted by the help of the prostitute Helena. <note>original: "Magus hæreſin condidit, Helenæ meretricis adjutus auxilio." Simon Magus, mentioned in the Book of Acts, was traditionally accompanied by Helena, whom he claimed was the first thought of his mind.</note> Nicholas of Antioch, the inventor of all impurities, led female choirs. Marcion sent a woman to Rome to prepare the minds of those he intended to deceive. Apelles had Philomene as a companion to his teachings. ## Of the Inspired Female Teachers, Prophetesses, Quakers, Enthusiasts, and Other Seductive and Suspicious Women.

# History and Description

**CATHERINE OF HALBERSTADT** (Halberstadiensis Catharina). This is one of the three well-known "inspired maids" <note>original German: *begeisterten Mägde*—young women within the Pietist movement who claimed to receive direct revelations or speak in tongues while in trances</note> about whom Magister August Hermann Francke <note>August Hermann Francke (1663–1727) was a prominent Lutheran clergyman and a central figure in the Pietist movement at the University of Halle</note>, Professor at Halle, composed a specific report. He sent this report to his confessor, David Ehrich, Pastor at Ammendorff near Halle, mentioning that he would like it returned soon so that Catherine’s inspiration might also be shared with other brothers and sisters. Through this report, the sharing of the information, and the gathering of Catherine’s letters, Professor Francke sufficiently revealed that he regarded her fanaticism <term>Fanaticismum: in this period, a label for those who claimed private revelation that superseded the Bible or the established Church</term>, her ecstasies, and her enthusiastic reveries <term>Schwermereyen: a derogatory term used by orthodox critics to describe what they saw as the irrational or delusional emotionalism of Pietist visionaries</term> as originating from the Holy Spirit and as being Divine. Bartholomæus Meyer, Superintendent at Wolfenbüttel, did exactly the same, expressing himself in a letter to Dr. Petersen <note>Johann Wilhelm Petersen (1649–1727), another key Pietist figure often criticized for his millenarian and visionary beliefs</note>: "Oh, that the Lord would further pour out His Spirit upon His maids in such a way as He has upon this Catherine of Halberstadt." See Dr. Samuel Schelwig’s *Sectarian Pietism* <note>original Latin: *Pietismus Sectarium*; Samuel Schelwig was a staunch defender of Lutheran Orthodoxy and a fierce critic of Francke and the Pietists</note>, part 2, page 227.

### of Catherine of Halberstadt.

### CHASBIA, or COZBIA.

# Of the Fells.

<meta>catchword: Eng-</meta>

Anyone who has looked into Quaker history even a little will have very often encountered the names of the **Fells**. <note>original: "Felliorum und Felliarum" - the author uses Latinized plural forms for the male and female members of the Fell family.</note> **Thomas Fell**, a distinguished judge, gave the "Arch-Quaker" **George Fox** free access to his house; it was through this man’s assistance that Quakerism spread so extensively. His wife, **Margaret Fell**, converted entirely to the Quakers; and while her husband outwardly remained with the Reformed Church, she, by contrast, not only preached within the Society of Friends herself, but also instructed others through various books she authored. The eldest son, **Leonard Fell**, likewise adopted the religion practiced by these people. He was soon followed by his brother, **Henry Fell**, who intended to spread these beliefs in the most remote lands toward the rising of the sun <note>A poetic way of referring to the East or the Orient.</note>. # History and Description

**CATHERINE FIESCHI** <note>original: "Catharina Fieschia"</note>. This is the well-known **Catherine of Genoa**, of whom mention will be made below. Otherwise, she is also called **Catherine Adorno** or **Adornavia**, because she was married to a nobleman in **Genoa**, **Giuliano Adorno** <note>original: "Julianum Adorno"</note>; with whom, however—as her *Biography, Halle edition, page 413* states—she experienced much misfortune and heartache during the ten years she spent with him, as he plunged her into great misery and poverty through his dissolute squandering of his estate. Her **fanaticism** <note>original: "Fanaticismo"; in this historical context, the term often refers to intense mystical experiences or radical piety that deviated from established church norms.</note> will be discussed shortly hereafter.

**REGINA FISCHER** <note>original: "Regina Fischeria"</note>. Nevertheless, he held a completely different opinion on this matter than the **Papists** <note>original: "Päbstler"; a historical, often polemical term for Roman Catholics.</note> do today. He believed that the souls of both the faithful and the unfaithful would have to pass through the purgatory that will consume the world at the **Last Judgment** <note>original: "Jüngsten Gericht"</note>. ### CATHARINA FORSTERIA

Love for prayer / makes its internal and external works into a means and instrumental cause of spiritual union; that she places rest not in God / but in a mere contemplation of the mind; that she believes one attains heaven through love for God / rather than through knowledge of God. ### History and Description

**MARGARETHA HEIDEWETTERIN**. Whoever opens the *Mirror of Penitence of Cottbus* <note>original Latin: *speculum pœnitentiæ Cotbusianum*</note>, which was printed in Leipzig in the year 1624, will receive a sufficient report of the ecstasies <note>original Latin: *ecstasibus*</note>, trances, and inspired speeches of this young girl from Cottbus in Lower Lusatia. From this source, Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714), a radical pietist historian known for his sympathetic view of "heretics"</note> has drawn what he presents in *Part 3 of the History, Section f, page 224* regarding Heidewetterin—namely, that in the eleventh year of her age, in the year 1629, she fell into severe distress <note>likely referring to a state of spiritual or physical crisis often associated with mystical visions</note>, and therein delivered all manner of beautiful, charming, and lovely speeches concerning the Lord Jesus; she also exhorted the people with great earnestness toward repentance, patience, and prayer. In her trances, great forthcoming trials over Germany were indicated by her, and how the Lord Jesus, in the greatest time of need, would finally help His own through the Swedish King and the relief <note>original: *Succurs*; referring to military reinforcements or aid</note> against the Papists <note>a derogatory term for Roman Catholics, common during the religious wars of the era</note>. Because of these things, Heidewetterin must now serve as a "witness of truth" to whom God particularly revealed Himself within the *History of Heretics*. I do not know, however, whether such matters withstand the test of scrutiny.

Sometimes he knocked on all the walls in the rooms; sometimes he swarmed around in the rooms; sometimes he was in the house, sometimes in the cellar, sometimes in the chamber; sometimes he rocked the child, sometimes he woke the boy, and so forth. This is exactly as if someone were to say: "I will not leave the room until it is proven to me that I am not an honest man." In such a case, that person would have to be branded a dishonest man, or else he would have to stay in the room until he died. # URSULA LEONHARDIA

When Melchior Hoffmann <note>A prominent radical Anabaptist leader who predicted the world would end in Strasbourg in 1533.</note> spread the fanatical swarm of Thomas Münzer <note>A radical reformer and leader during the German Peasants' War whose followers were often associated with social upheaval.</note> along the Rhine and troubled the city of Strasbourg with his **religious enthusiasm** and **Anabaptist** <note>original: *Wiedertäuffer*; a movement that advocated for adult baptism and was often persecuted by both Catholics and other Protestants.</note> doctrines in the year 1532, the local authorities sought a beneficial remedy against this and threw Hoffmann into prison. 

While there, he caused a great sensation because of many alleged **visions**, which his faithful companion-in-arms Jodocus Leonhardi—or as others call him, Leonhard Jodocus—published after his death. Through such supposed divine visions, he gained considerable standing among the common people, so that not only the men, such as Cornelius Poltermann, but also the women—specifically Leonhardi’s wife, **Ursula**—revered him as an incomparable man of God. They spread his heresy among the people like a poisonous soul-powder of the Devil. According to the testimony of Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a Catholic cardinal and historian famous for his massive history of the church, the *Annales Ecclesiastici*.</note>, volume 19 of his *Annals* for the year 1532.

# HISTORY AND DESCRIPTION

In 1532, as recorded on folio 840, the Anabaptist woman **Leonhardi** <note>Ursula Leonhardi, wife of Jodocus Leonhardi; she was a central figure in the circle of "Strasbourg prophets."</note> prophesied that Hoffmann was Elijah, while Poltermann was Enoch <note>In radical millenarian theology, the return of the biblical prophets Elijah and Enoch was expected to herald the end of the world.</note>, and that Strasbourg <note>original: *Argentoratum*</note> was the chosen Zion. She claimed to have seen a great multitude of brothers and sisters gathered in proper order in a very large hall; a boy entered there, dressed in a white garment, who carried around a golden bowl filled with a most excellent drink to everyone; however, it was emptied by no one except Cornelius [Poltermann], who was the true Enoch. Because of these and many other strange prophecies, Ursula is counted among the false prophetesses, about which one can read more in Plarrius’s *Historical Specimens of the Anabaptists* <note>original: *specimen Historiæ Anabapt.*</note>, chapter 6, page 46.

Another inspired woman named **Barbara** sought to support Ursula, alleging that she saw a white swan swimming here and there in a clear river, and from time to time singing of the mystery of the vision; she claimed this swan was Hoffmann, who would shortly appear with Poltermann and gather the faithful with his sweet preaching. ### LIBUINA

By some, she is called **Lidwina**, by others **Lydwida** or **Lydwidis**. We are not so much concerned with her actual name as with her errors and fanatical nature. Regarding this, Voetius <term>Volume 2, *Selected Disputations*, p. 1066</term> <note>Gisbertus Voetius (1589–1676) was a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian known for his opposition to mysticism and "fanaticism"</note> provides this report from Brugman and Surius <note>Johannes Brugman and Laurentius Surius were 15th and 16th-century biographers who wrote lives of the saints, including Saint Lydwine of Schiedam</note>: that she claimed many divine visions, heavenly revelations, and holy conversations with angels. However, everything that Libuina claimed was either a fictional invention of the monks or, as Voetius maintains in the place cited <note>original: *l. c.* (loco citato)</note>, a deception of the Devil, to which one should pay no attention at all.

## LUNA <note>Latin for "The Moon"</note>

This is Helena, the "house-prophetess" of the sorcerer Simon Magus. She is called *Selene* <note>Greek: σελήνη, meaning Moon</note>—or in Latin, *Luna*—by Irenaeus <note>An early Church Father and writer against heresies</note>, who lived around the year 185 AD, in his *Recognitions, book 2, p. 31*. However, it is almost impossible to believe that this seductive woman ever actually bore the name of "the Moon" [Lunae]. Rather, I agree with Ludovico Vives <note>A famous Spanish humanist and scholar</note> in his *Commentary on Augustine’s 'On Heresies', p. 48*, that through the misunderstanding or negligence of a scribe—who should have written *Helena* [ἑλένη]—the word *Selene* [σελήνη] crept in alongside it.

## LUTGARDIS

# MATHILDIS #

Regarding this woman, most writers note that she was a very wealthy lady from Italy and a first cousin of Emperor Henry IV. She was a bold and audacious woman, much like the ancient Amazons <note>A legendary race of female warriors in Greek mythology; here used to describe Matilda's assertive and military character.</note>. For this reason, she even obtained permission from the Pope to personally attend the councils <note>Formal meetings of church leaders to establish doctrine or discipline.</note> and assemblies of the clergy. Within these meetings, however, through her clever intrigues, she introduced and confirmed many superstitious things in church affairs. 

The unusual intimacy which she maintained with Pope Hildebrand <note>Better known as Pope Gregory VII (reigned 1073–1085), he was a major reformer but also a highly controversial figure who fought for papal supremacy.</note> appeared to most as if they loved one another more carnally than spiritually—or, as the words of Lambert <note>Lambert of Hersfeld was an 11th-century historian whose chronicles are a primary, though often biased, source for the history of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> state: "that day and night the Pope shamelessly wallowed in the embraces of Matilda; and she, preoccupied by her secret love for the Pope, after the loss of her husband, refused to enter into a second marriage" <note>original: "quod die ac nocte impudenter Papa in Mathildis volutaretur amplexibus; & hæc, furtivis Papæ amoribus præoccupata, post amissum conjugem, ultra secundas contrahere nuptias."</note>.

### PRISCILLA.

No one should think that by this name we mean the wife of Aquila (1 Corinthians 16:19; 2 Timothy 4:19). For since that woman was a helper to the Apostle Paul (Romans 16:3) and moreover diligently explained the way of God (Acts 18:26), it follows of itself that a different Priscilla must be the subject here. This Priscilla is the second "house-prophetess" <note>term: *Hausprophetin*. A title used for women in radical religious groups who claimed to receive direct revelations within their community.</note> of **Montanus**. Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403) was a bishop known for his "Panarion," a massive work cataloging and refuting various heresies.</note> calls Montanus a wretched little man <note>original Greek: *eleeinon anthrōparion*</note> (*Heresies 48, number 11*). Montanus knew how to praise Priscilla's revelations to the people so highly that he held them above the divine Gospel <note>original Greek: *hyper to theion euangelion*</note>, placing them higher than the writings of the Holy Evangelists. As Henningus Witte reports to us in his *Biographical Diary for the year 1624*, <note>original Latin: *Diar. ### S.
ELIZABETH of SCHÖNAU.
This female figure lived in the 12th century as Abbess of Schönau in the Diocese <note>original German: "Stifft" — an ecclesiastical territory under the jurisdiction of a bishop or monastery.</note> of Trier, where she became very famous for her alleged visions and revelations. Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>original Latin: "Jacobus Faber Stapulensis" — a French humanist and theologian.</note> first published these in Paris in the year 1513, preferring them over all other visions and revelations <note>original Latin: "visionibus und revelationibus"</note> of inspired women. Nevertheless, other Catholic writers <note>original German: "Päbstler" — a period-specific term for "Papists," often used in a sectarian context.</note> such as Gobelinus Persona, Barthol. Sybilla, Henricus de Hassia, etc., regard them as false and fictional, and for this reason they wish to know nothing of Elizabeth's holiness. See Voetius <note>Gisbertus Voetius, a prominent Dutch Reformed theologian.</note> *volume 3, Select Disputations, page 495.* These people are more cautious and clever in this matter than Gottfried Arnold <note>A radical pietist historian known for his sympathetic view of "heretics."</note>, who, in his *Mystical Theology, page 515* and in his *Defense, page 202*, titles the woman of Schönau as an enlightened and holy female person. However, Arnold should have considered: (1.) that this person lived at such a time when, with superstition having reached its peak <note>original Greek: <unclear>ἀκμὴν</unclear></note>, people everywhere were raving about dreams, visions, and signs; as Voetius—

But their singing of "Hosanna" and "Holy, Holy, Holy," combined with the gathering of the crowd, was of such a nature that they could hardly be examined that night. For this reason, they were held in Newgate <note>Newgate Prison in Bristol, a notorious place of confinement for religious dissenters in the 17th century.</note> until the following day. On October 25th, Naylor was examined, and he was very quick with his answers; yet, when he noticed that he might be trapped by a question, he preferred to remain silent, or answered subtly, or denied certain things that were presented to him. The Magistrate of Bristol sent Naylor to London with his female companions. On November 15th, the Commission convened and questioned Naylor:

## II. Index.

**Arnoldus (Nicolaus)** reprimands Comenius for defending the enthusiasts. 242. <note>original: *Schwärmer*. Nicolaus Arnoldus was a Reformed theologian known for his polemics; Jan Amos Comenius was a famous educator and bishop of the Moravian Brethren.</note>
**Augustine** on the Donatist heretics 426. Judgment of his book on heresies 504. is revised by the Benedictine monks in Paris 504. is the best teacher after the age of the Apostles. 505.

->B.<-

**Bader (Johann Georg)** allows himself to be led astray by his daughter 56. and by Asseburg. 147. <note>Rosamunde Juliane von der Asseburg was a well-known visionary and prophetess whose claims of direct revelation influenced many early Pietists.</note>
**Labadie (Jean de)** an enthusiast 594, 596. is praised by Dr. Spener 594. leads Schurman astray. 594. <note>Jean de Labadie was a French mystic; Anna Maria van Schurman, a famous scholar, gave up her academic life to join his communal sect.</note>
**Barthius (Caspar)** on the devil's comedy.
**Basiliscus (Emperor)** an Eutychian. 671. <note>Followers of Eutyches believed that Christ had only one nature—a divine one—rather than being both fully human and fully divine.</note>
**Peasant-shrewdness** a fountainhead of errors 15.
**Inspired maidens** 53. their patron is Francke at Halle 53. and B. Meyer 220. and Achilles 221. and Sprögel 555, 589. they elevate the Pietists. 117. <note>original: *Begeiſterte Mägde*. Critics of Pietism often pointed to young women claiming prophetic visions as proof that the movement was based on emotionalism rather than sound doctrine.</note>
**Benzen (Siegfried)** reveals the deceptions of Peters 467, 478. thinks nothing of the word "heretic-maker" 601. his account of Schwarz. 611. <note>original: *Ketzermacher*. A term used by the historian Gottfried Arnold to criticize orthodox theologians who were quick to label any deviation as heresy.</note>
**Beverland (Hadrian)** a lewd writer. 131. <note>original: *priapæus*. Referring to the Roman god Priapus; Beverland was an author whose works on original sin were considered scandalous and obscene in the 17th century.</note>

## II. Index.

**Bücher (Friedrich Christian)** rails against the book-writing of Mrs. Petersen 100, 462. and English writings 416. <note>Friedrich Christian Bücher was a Lutheran theologian who criticized Johanna Eleonora Petersen, one of the few prominent female theologians of the Pietist movement.</note>
**Bourdelot** <note>original: *Burdelotius*</note> leads Queen Christina astray. 224. <note>Pierre Michon Bourdelot was a French physician whose influence over Queen Christina of Sweden during her residence in Rome was a subject of much scandal.</note>
**Burnet (Gilbert)** on the deception of women. 173. <note>Gilbert Burnet was a well-known Scottish theologian and Bishop of Salisbury.</note>

->**C.**<-

**Caecilianus** rails against Lucilla. 414. <note>Caecilianus was a 4th-century Bishop of Carthage; his conflict with the wealthy noblewoman Lucilla helped spark the Donatist schism.</note>
**Calixtus (Friedrich Ulrich)** on the ecstasies of women 105. on the gatherings of the Pietists. 267. writes against Jane Leade 371. <note>original: *die Janin*. Jane Leade was an English mystic whose "Philadelphian" writings had a significant impact on German Pietists.</note>
**Catechizing** <note>original: *Catechisation*</note> belongs to women. 102.
**Carpocrates** <note>original: *Corporates*</note> makes use of women for his heresy. 46, 433. <note>Carpocrates was an early Gnostic teacher; the author here links ancient heresy with the contemporary Pietist reliance on female visionaries.</note>
**Carpzov (Johann Benedict)** academic discourse on the Pietistic colleges. 268. <note>original: *Programma von den Collegiis Pietisticis*. These "colleges" were the private Bible study circles or conventicles central to Pietism.</note>
**Carpzov (Samuel Benedict)** complaint regarding the misleading of women. 18.
**La Chaise (Father)** incites persecution in France 116. <note>Père de La Chaise was the Jesuit confessor to King Louis XIV, often blamed by Protestants for the revocation of the Edict of Nantes.</note>
**Chemnitz (Martin)** uncovers the sources of heresy. 15. <note>original: *Fontes Hæreseos*. Martin Chemnitz was a foundational Lutheran theologian known for his systematic defense of the faith.</note>
**Millenarians** <note>original: *Chiliastæ*</note> their hope for better times. 3, 578. their defender is Dr. Petersen 52, along with Mrs. Frölich 299. and Liese of Erfurt 557. <note>Millenarianism is the belief in a future thousand-year reign of Christ on earth. "Liese of Erfurt" refers to Elisabeth of Erfurt, a servant girl who claimed to have prophetic visions.</note>
**Chrysostom** on the imprudence of women. 111. rebukes Eudoxia 461. <note>John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" preacher, was famously exiled after criticizing the Roman Empress Eudoxia.</note>

**Colberg (Timotheus Daniel)** is attacked by Arnold 407. is well-read in Fanatical Theology 436. his report on Quaker-Powder 586. <note>Timotheus Daniel Colberg was a Lutheran theologian who wrote against "fanatics" and Pietists. ### D.

### A Brief Notice.

This refutation was prepared only as a preface to a detailed small treatise *concerning the Arnoldian Adepts* <note>original Latin: *de adeptis Arnoldinis*. In this context, "adepts" refers to those initiated into Arnold’s mystical or radical teachings.</note>, which was intended to appear at the upcoming Michaelmas Fair <note>one of the two major annual book trade fairs in Leipzig, occurring in late September.</note>. However, because such subject matter is best suited to the *Fanatical Women’s Quarters* <note>original Latin: *Gynæceo fanatico*; a derogatory term used by Feustking to describe the circles of female visionaries and prophets associated with Radical Pietism.</note>, it has been placed here as an appendix and left to the kind reader as a conclusion, which may be followed hereafter by the *History of Arnoldian Libertinism* <note>original Latin: *Historia Libertinismi Arnoldini*.</note>.

<meta>catchword: Now</meta>

<summary>In this brief preface, Feustking explains that this text was originally intended as an introduction to a larger work on Arnold’s followers but was instead appended to his current volume on "fanatical" women.</summary>
<keywords>Michaelmas Fair, Arnoldian Adepts, Fanatical Gynaeceum, Johann Heinrich Feustking, Gottfried Arnold, publication history, religious polemics</keywords>

# Jesus, Help Further! <note>original German: "JEsu Hilff Ferner!" This is a traditional pious invocation commonly found at the beginning of early modern Lutheran theological texts.</note>

->§. I.<-

Gottfried Arnold <note>Gottfried Arnold (1666–1714) was a radical Pietist historian whose work "Impartial History of the Church and Heretics" scandalized the Lutheran establishment by arguing that "heretics" were often truer Christians than the institutional church.</note> is in the habit of attaching various supplements, additions, extras, appendices—or whatever they may be called—to his writings. This is clearly seen in the conclusion of his *History of Heretics*, in his *Life of the Believers*, and in his *Spiritual Form of a Teacher* <note>original German titles: "Ketzer-Historie," "Leben der Gläubigen," and "Geistlichen Gestalt eines Lehrers." These were Arnold’s most influential and controversial works.</note>. In this regard, we wish to follow his example this time and include this refutation as an appendix to the *Fanatical Women’s Quarters* <note>original Latin: "Gynæceo fanatico." Feustking uses this term to mock the circles of female prophets and mystics associated with Arnold.</note> for this reason: so that his damned free-thinking <term>Freygeisterey: a derogatory term for radical religious views that departed from established church dogma, often equated with atheism or libertinism</term> may be increasingly exposed and thwarted.

§. II. For such free-thinking, as has been frequently noted, is the true focal point toward which all the writings of Gottfried Arnold aim—especially his two folio volumes of the *History of Heretics*, which he compiled from the works of so many teachers of the devil <note>original German: "Teuffels-Lehrern." Feustking is asserting that Arnold's "impartial" history is actually a collection of demonic heresies.</note>—aiming <note>The text ends mid-sentence with "abzielen," which translates to "to aim at."</note>

<summary>Feustking explains that he is adding this refutation as an appendix to mimic Gottfried Arnold's own publishing habits. He characterizes Arnold’s famous "History of Heretics" as a dangerous collection of "devilish" teachings designed to promote radical free-thinking.</summary>
<keywords>Gottfried Arnold, History of Heretics, Pietism, free-thinking, religious polemics, Fanatical Women's Quarters, Johann Heinrich Feustking</keywords>

### Short Notice.

This refutation was prepared only as a foreword to a detailed little treatise *concerning the Arnoldian initiates* <note>original Latin: "de adeptis Arnoldinis." The "adepts" were the inner circle or dedicated followers of Gottfried Arnold’s radical mystical teachings.</note>, which was intended to appear at the coming Michaelmas Fair <note>The Michaelmas Fair in Leipzig was one of the most important annual events for the German book trade, where new scholarly and theological works were debuted.</note>. Because such material is best suited for the *Fanatical Women’s Quarters* <note>original Latin: "Gynæceo fanatico." This is the Latin title of the book this page belongs to, in which Feustking attacks female prophets and mystics.</note>, it has been placed here as an appendix and left for the kind reader as a conclusion, which the *History of Arnoldian Libertinism* <note>original Latin: "Historia Libertinismi Arnoldini." Feustking used the term "libertinism" to suggest that Arnold's followers lacked proper religious and moral discipline.</note> may follow after this.

This is how the incomparable **exegete** <note>one who provides critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially scripture</note>, the late **Egidius Hunnius** <note>1550–1603; a leading Lutheran theologian who defended orthodoxy against Calvinism and internal dissent</note>, glossed and noted regarding this passage: <note>original Latin: "quod hic de fœminis prophetantibus habetur, plane fuit extraordinarium quid, ad eorum temporum rationes congruens, ubi Spiritus Sanctus visibiliter illabebatur non in viros solum, sed etiam in mulieres, ut loquerentur linguis & prophetarent."</note> "What is held here concerning women prophesying was clearly something extraordinary, suited to the conditions of those times, when the **Holy Spirit** visibly descended not only upon men, but also upon women, so that they might speak in tongues and prophesy." Thus, **Mr. Arnold** should see that such a passage cannot at all be applied to the present-day prophesying of his **female adepts** <note>original: *adeptarum*; a term for his female followers who claimed direct spiritual illumination</note>.

### Refutation of the Objections /
<meta>catchword: planted</meta>

...[churches that the Apostles] planted ceased? This objection is of the same nature as if I were to say: If there were **Apostles** and female **Apostles** <note>original: *Apostolinnen*; referring to the women who assisted the early messengers of the Gospel</note> at the beginning of the **New Testament** who went out into all the world, why should we not also be able to have the same in our current times?

However, the **Apostolic office**—and the practice of going out into all the world, in which the sisters whom the Apostles took with them as their traveling companions also participated (**1 Corinthians 9:5**) —was a **personal privilege** <note>original Latin: *privilegium personäle*; a legal or ecclesiastical right granted to a specific person rather than an office</note> that was only intended to last for a limited time. It was not meant to be inherited by **successors** <note>original Latin: *successores*</note> in later times. 

Otherwise, by virtue of such a custom, each and every **preacher** would still have to be an **Apostle** and go out into all the world. Yet this does not happen, nor must it happen, because every **pastor** is now obligated to remain with his specific church, to which he has been **ordinarily called** <note>referring to the *vocatio ordinaria*, the formal process of being assigned to a specific parish rather than traveling as a missionary</note>.

The same situation applied to the office of the **prophets** and to the **extraordinary gift of prophecy** <note>the divine inspiration to reveal God's will or future events</note>; while these were indeed common in the **Early Church**, they were not intended to be continued in the **Latter Church**. But that in the beginning...

<summary>The author argues that early church roles, like the Apostles and female prophets, were temporary "personal privileges" of that era rather than permanent offices. He concludes that modern pastors are called to specific congregations rather than the wandering ministry of the Apostolic age.</summary>

# Refutation and Objections / for etc.

If he chooses to thunder against me, to slander me, or—as has already happened several times by others—to harass my person with all sorts of **Pietistic lampoons**, <note>original: *Pasquinaden*. A "pasquinade" is a public satire or lampoon, often posted in a public place. In this period, religious disputes were often fought through such anonymous, biting pamphlets.</note> let him do so on his own responsibility. I will gladly suffer such things for the sake of God’s honor; however, I will refuse certain things for my own sake, defending the truth as best as I can. Yet, to spite my enemies, I will also laugh at various things and then complain of what remains to the **just authorities**. <note>original: *Obrigkeit*. This refers to the local government or ruling magistrates who held the power to enforce religious and civil order.</note> I conclude with these words from the **26th Psalm**: <note>The author is quoting a versified hymn based on Psalm 26:4-5, which expresses the believer's desire to remain separate from the ungodly.</note>

> With people who are not upright,
> I cannot remain at one,
> I hate from the bottom of my heart,
> Those by whom **false doctrine** <note>original: *falsche Lehre*. In the context of this book, "false doctrine" specifically refers to the radical "inspirations" and mystical teachings of the Pietists that the author views as heretical.</note> is spun;
> I guard myself against their deed,
> Into their counsel my soul shall not proceed,
> I wish to die as their enemy!
